evidence.ruling_summary: Breach of Clause 4.1 (omission of prescribing information), Breach of Clause 4.3 (failure to provide non-proprietary name adjacent to the brand name on first mention), and Breach of Clause 10.1 (failure of written promotional material to state that it was sponsored by the company, though the invitation stated sponsorship, but email delivery issues arose; specifically breach found for omission of prescribing info and generic name requirements).
Breach of Clauses 7.2 and 7.4; No breach of Clause 4.1.
Breach of Clauses 15.2 and 20.1; No breach of Clause 2.
No breach of Clause 15.4, Clause 9.1, and Clause 2.

Breach of Clauses 3.2, 7.2, 7.3, 7.8, and 8.1 found in relation to claims regarding the role of complexing proteins, cold chain storage advantages/disparagement, and 1:1 dose comparability with Botox in light of SPC statements on non-interchangeability.
Breach of Clause 7.2 ruled.
Breach of Clause 18.1, Breach of Clause 9.1, and Breach of Clause 2.
Breach of Clause 19.1 and Clause 9.1. No breach of Clause 2.
Breach of Clause 7.2, Clause 8.1, and Clause 9.1. No breach of Clause 2.
Breach of Clauses 7.2, 7.4, and 9.1; No breach of Clause 2.
Breach of Clauses 7.2, 7.3 and 9.1 found for misleading promotional material comparing the morphine equivalence of Targinact to co-codamol; no breach of Clause 2.
Breach of Clauses 3.2, 11.1 and 15.2. No breach of Clause 15.9.

No breach of Clause 9.4 was ruled. The Panel considered that while there were some conceptual similarities, the advertisements were sufficiently distinct and the products were clearly identified such that the advertisement was not an imitation likely to mislead or confuse.
No breach of Clauses 7.2 and 15.2.
Breach of Clauses 7.2 and 9.1; No breach of Clauses 2, 18.1 and 18.4.
Breach of Clause 3.2, Clause 7.2 and Clause 7.9; No breach of Clause 2.
Breach of Clause 3.2, Clause 9.1, and Clause 15.2; No breach of Clause 2.
Breach of Clauses 3.2, 4.1, 4.10, 9.1, and 12.1; No breach of Clause 2.

No breach of Clause 9.1, Clause 9.7, or Clause 22.1. The Panel considered that the provision of the proprietary flavoured iced drink (Slush Puppie) was modest refreshment secondary to the main purpose of the scientific congress and did not constitute an improper inducement or fail to maintain high standards.
No breach of Clause 15.1, Clause 9.1, and Clause 2.

Breach of Clauses 3.2, 9.1, and 12.1 found for promoting empagliflozin in a manner inconsistent with its summary of product characteristics (prior to the grant of a cardiovascular risk reduction indication) and using a letter format resembling an urgent non-promotional communication (disguised promotion). No breach of Clause 2 was ruled.
Breach of Clauses 2, 9.1 and 29 ruled for failure to comply with an undertaking given in a previous case (Case AUTH/2802/11/15).

No breach of Clauses 2, 9.1, 18.1, and 18.4 of the 2014 Code. The Panel found that Bristol-Myers Squibb had established appropriate processes and requirements for the patient support service, which was initiated by the treating hospital, and there was no evidence that the company had failed to maintain high standards or breached the Code.
No breach of Clauses 2, 3.1, 3.2, and 9.1

No breach of Clauses 2, 9.1, 22.1, and 22.2 was ruled. The Panel considered that the venue (St George's House, Windsor Castle) and arrangements were appropriate and not lavish or extravagant, and that Servier had conducted appropriate due diligence regarding its sponsorship of the educational meeting.
Breach of Clauses 3.1, 4.1, 9.1, 14.3, 26.1, and 28.1. No breach of Clause 2 and Clause 4.6.
No breach of the Code was ruled, including no breach of Clauses 2, 3.2, 7.2, 9.1, 15.9, 18.1, 19.1, 19.2, and 23.1.

Breach of Clause 9.1 ruled. The Panel considered that MSD had failed to honour an inter-company undertaking to withdraw promotional materials associating alogliptin with an inverted black triangle by the end of August 2018, and had thereby failed to maintain high standards.

Breach of Clauses 3.2, 7.2, and 9.1 ruled by the Panel. The FAQ responses did not reflect the SPC, encouraged off-label use/inconsistent use, and failed to maintain high standards. No breach of Clause 2 was ruled.

No breach of Clauses 2, 9.1, 12.1, and 19.2 was ruled. The Panel found that the third-party provider's internal email, while using poorly chosen wording, did not demonstrate that GlaxoSmithKline's sponsored therapy review service was linked to prescribing of its products or that the service failed to meet the requirements of the Code.
Breach of Clauses 4.1, 9.1, and 16.3; No breach of Clause 16.1.
Breach of Clauses 9.1, 22.1 and 22.2. No breach of Clauses 2, 16.1 and 16.3.

Breach of Clauses 2, 9.1, 24.1, 24.4, 24.6, 24.7, 24.9, and 24.10 ruled due to significant failures in accurately documenting and disclosing transfers of value to healthcare professionals for attendance at the 2018 ESC congress on Disclosure UK.
Breach of Clauses 4.1, 4.6, 7.2, 7.3, 9.1, and 12.1; No Breach of Clause 2, Clause 4.9, and Clause 14.1.
Breach of Clause 9.1 and Clause 12.1. No breach of Clause 2.
Breach of Clause 27.9 and Clause 9.1. No breach of Clause 27.3 and Clause 2.
No breach of Clause 9.1 and No breach of Clause 11.1 was ruled by the Panel.
Breach of Clauses 26.1, 26.2, and 9.1; No breach of Clause 2.
Breach of Clause 4.1 and Clause 9.1

No breach of Clauses 2, 3.1, 9.1 and 11.1. The Panel found that Lundbeck had provided factual, non-promotional pipeline information in response to a standard request from the Specialist Pharmacy Service (SPS) to assist with NHS horizon scanning, and this did not constitute the promotion of an unlicensed medicine.
Breach of Clause 3.1 and Clause 9.1; No breach of Clause 2.
Breach of Clauses 3.1, 9.1, 26.1, 29, and 2 found.

Breach of Clause 5.1 ruled for failing to maintain high standards by providing an 0845 number (a higher-rate call number) for members of the public/patients to report adverse events on the Saxenda website. No breach of Clause 6.1 was ruled.
Breach of Clause 2, Clause 4.2, Clause 9.1, and Clause 29 ruled by the Panel.

Breach of Clauses 5.1, 6.1, and 6.2 found regarding misleading and unsubstantiated comparisons of adverse events across the trials. No breach of Clause 11.2 was found regarding the discussion of conventional versus novel (PSMA-PET) imaging and licensed indications, and no breach of Clause 2 was ruled.

No breach of Clauses 24.2, 19.1, 5.1, and 2 of the 2021 Code was ruled. The Panel concluded that AstraZeneca (and Daiichi Sankyo in AUTH/3635/4/22) demonstrated a genuine, legitimate business need for the UK advisory board on trastuzumab deruxtecan and that it was not disguised promotion.
Breach of Clauses 5.1, 6.1, 6.2, 11.2, and 12.1. No breach of Clause 2.
Breaches of Clauses 4.1, 4.3 and 10.1.
No breach of Clause 4.1, breach of Clause 7.2, breach of Clause 7.4
No breach of Clause 20.3

The Panel ruled that Lilly had promoted a prescription-only medicine to the public and in so doing had brought discredit upon, and reduced confidence in, the pharmaceutical industry. Breaches of the Code were ruled.
The Panel ruled breaches of Clauses 7.2, 7.3, 9.1 and 22 but no breach of Clause 2.

Novartis Pharmaceuticals UK Ltd was ruled in breach of Clauses 3.2, 7.2, 7.3, 7.4, 7.10, and 20.2 of the ABPI Code of Practice. The Panel found the leavepiece for Femara (letrozole) misleading because it presented unbalanced data on efficacy in patient subgroups and omitted important safety information, and made unjustified claims about the scope of its marketing authorisation.

The Panel ruled a breach of Clause 20.1 (advertising of prescription-only medicines to the public) and no breach of Clauses 2 (bringing discredit upon the industry) and 15.2 (providing information to the public).
Breach of Clause 7.2
Breach of Clauses 9.1 and 9.9, no breach of Clause 12.2
Breach of Clause 19.1 for the nightclub venue; no breach of Clause 19.1 for the wax museum; no breach of Clause 9.1.

The Panel ruled breaches of the Code including Clauses 2, 7.2, 7.4, and 9.1 for a letter promoting Dovobet which misleadingly implied a direct switch from Dovonex was appropriate, lacked fair balance regarding corticosteroid risks, and brought discredit on the industry.
The Panel ruled no breach of Clauses 7.2, 11.4. The Panel ruled a breach of Clause 11.4 in relation to presentation of data from Currie et al.
No Breach of Clauses 2, 9.1 and 15.4.

The Panel ruled breaches of the Code including Clause 4.1 because the non-proprietary name was not in a sufficiently large font size immediately adjacent to the most prominent display of the brand name.
The Panel ruled breaches of Clauses 7.2, 8.1, 3.2 and 7.2 of the Code.
The Panel ruled breaches of Clauses 2, 10, 18.1 and 18.4 of the 2006 Code.
The Panel ruled that the claim breached Clause 7.2 as it was misleading, but did not breach Clauses 3.2, 7.4 and 7.10.
Breaches of Clauses 2, 9.1 and 19.1 were ruled.
The Panel ruled breaches of Clauses 9.1, 14.1, 15.9, and 16.2 for uncertified training materials and inadequate training on the Code and company policies.
The Panel ruled breaches of Clauses 7.2, 8.1 and 9.1. No breach of Clause 2 was ruled.

No breach of Clauses 2, 7.2, 7.4 and 9.1. The letter from Lundbeck was not misleading. The panel considered the PCT newsletter and Lundbeck’s letter were different documents aimed at different audiences. The newsletter was clear that escitalopram was not a formulary drug. The letter from Lundbeck was consistent with the newsletter as it referred to the occasions when escitalopram would be used. It did not state, or imply, that it had been added to the formulary.
The Panel ruled that the promotional material was misleading and in breach of Clauses 2, 7.2, 7.3 and 9.1 of the Code.
GlaxoSmithKline was ruled in breach of Clauses 9.1 and 12.1 for failing to make the scientific and promotional nature of the meeting clear on the invitation. No breach was ruled for Clauses 2 or 4.1.
Breaches of Clauses 3.2 and 11.1 ruled; no breaches of Clauses 15.2 and 15.9.
The Panel ruled no breach of Clause 9.4. The Eczmol advertisement was not an imitation of the Locoid advertisements that was likely to mislead or confuse.
The Panel ruled a breach of Clause 4.1.
No breach of Clauses 2, 9.1, and 18.1; breaches of Clauses 7.2 and 18.4 ruled
The Panel ruled a breach of Clause 7.2 because the material was not sufficiently balanced, failing to mention that Ferinject itself could cause hypersensitivity reactions.
The Panel ruled breaches of Clauses 3.2, 4.1, 7.2 and 9.1.
The Panel ruled breaches of the 2019 ABPI Code including Clauses 3.1, 3.2, 4.1, 9.1 and 2.
Breach of Clauses 7.2 and 7.3.
Breach of Clauses 14.1 and 14.5 for an out-of-date approval statement on the company website.
The Panel ruled breaches of Clauses 2, 9.1 and 9.9 of the Code.

The Panel ruled breaches of Clauses 7.2, 7.4, and 9.1 for the claim '... for an extra fine day', as it misleadingly suggested an unsubstantiated efficacy benefit linking the extra-fine formulation to a better day.
Breaches of Clauses 7.2 and 9.1 were ruled.

For GlaxoSmithKline, no breach of Clauses 1.8, 2, 9, and 21.3 of the Second 2012 Edition. The Panel determined GSK had posted summary results on its own register within 12 months, satisfying disclosure requirements; the study did not capture this, so no breach was ruled.
Panel ruled breaches of Clauses 12.1, 3.2, 2, and 9.1; no breach of Clauses 4.1 and 4.10.
Breach of Clauses 18.1 and 2.
The Panel ruled that Mallinckrodt breached Clauses 18.1 and 2 by offering contrast injectors as an inducement, which was not fair and reasonable and brought discredit upon the industry.
Breaches of Clauses 9.1 and 22.1, no breach of Clause 9.7
The Panel ruled breaches of Clauses 2, 3.2, 9.1 and 12.1.
The Panel ruled breaches of Clauses 7.2 and 9.1 and no breach of Clause 7.4.
No breach of Clauses 2, 3.1, 3.2 and 9.1
The Panel ruled breaches of Clauses 3.2, 9.1, 15.2, and 15.9 of the 2019 Code.

Shield Therapeutics was ruled in breach of the following clauses of the 2021 ABPI Code of Practice: Clause 2 - Bringing discredit upon, and reducing confidence in, the pharmaceutical industry; Clause 3.1 - Failing to ensure that its website did not include information that was inconsistent with the summary of product characteristics; Clause 4.1 - Failing to include prescribing information; Clause 4.6 - Failing to make information available to the public in a factual and balanced way and implying that a medicine could be recommended to the public; Clause 9.1 - Failing to maintain high standards; Clause 14.3 - Promoting medicines prior to the grant of a marketing authorization; Clause 26.1 - Failing to certify promotional material; and Clause 28.1 - Failing to ensure that material relating to medicines and their uses was factual and not misleading. The Panel ruled no breach of Clause 2 in relation to a misleading impression. No breach of Clause 2 was ruled as it was considered a sign of particular care that the company sought advice on promotional status, although other rulings of a breach of Clause 2 were made. No breach of Clause 4.1 for one page due to no mention of a specific product.

The Panel ruled breaches of the Code including Clauses 2, 9.1, 15.9, 18.1, and 19.1 for the first matter, finding that GSK engaged in a pre-planned promotional switch campaign orchestrated with a pharmacist using an inappropriate Q&A format and inadequate disclosure of transfers of value; for the second matter, the Panel ruled no breach of Clauses 3.2, 7.2, and 9.1 regarding the Ellipta device 'open, inhale, close' messaging.
No breach of the Code.

The Panel ruled breaches of Clauses 4.1, 4.2, 9.1, 11.1, 22.1, 26.1 and 28.1 for a Facebook advertisement for a diabetes specialist nurse meeting that lacked a sponsorship statement and prescribing information.
Breaches of Clauses 3.2, 7.2, and 9.1 ruled; no breach of Clause 2.

The Panel ruled that the claim 'Better tolerated than DTG-containing regimens' was misleading, not fair and balanced, and could not be substantiated, breaching Clauses 7.2, 7.3, 7.4 and 7.10. The rose and thorn imagery implied a safety advantage for Biktarvy which was not supported, breaching Clauses 7.2, 7.4, 7.9 and 8.1. The claim 'The beauty of what is possible... Biktarvy... is now a reality' suggested special merit for Biktarvy and was misleading, breaching Clauses 7.3 and 7.10. The Panel did not find evidence that the materials brought the industry into disrepute (Clause 2), but the breaches of Clauses 7.2, 7.3, 7.4, 7.9, 7.10 and 8.1 were ruled as breaches of Clause 9.1 (failure to maintain high standards).
The Panel ruled breaches of Clauses 4.1, 4.2, 4.4, 4.6, 4.9, 9.1, and 2.

The Panel ruled breaches of Clauses 2, 9.1 and 12.1 of the Code. GlaxoSmithKline failed to maintain high standards and failed to ensure that a third party acting on its behalf complied with the Code. No breach of Clause 19.2 was ruled.

The Panel ruled breaches of the 2016 Code including Clauses 2 (bringing discredit upon the pharmaceutical industry), 9.1 (failing to maintain high standards), and 12.1 (disguising promotional material). No breach of Clause 19.2 was ruled.
The Panel ruled breaches of Clauses 2, 9.1, 16.1, 16.3, 22.1 and 22.2.
The Panel ruled a breach of Clause 7.2 but no breach of Clause 7.10.
The Panel ruled breaches of Clauses 2, 9.1, 22.5, 24.1, 24.4, 24.6, 24.7, 24.9 and 24.10.

The Panel ruled breaches of Clauses 12.1, 4.1, 4.6, 4.9, 7.2, 7.3 and 9.1; no breaches of Clauses 2 and 14.1. The ivironheart.co.uk website was found to be disguised promotion and lacked prescribing information and adverse event reporting.

The Panel ruled no breach of the Code. It considered that the materials were promotional and did not constitute disguised promotion, as the promotional nature was apparent from the context and the link to prescribing information.
The Panel ruled breaches of Clauses 3.1, 26.1, 26.2 and 2.
The Panel ruled a breach of Clause 4.1 as the prescribing information on the detail aid was not the most up to date version.
The Panel ruled breaches of the Code including Clauses 2, 3.1, 9.1 and 11.1.
The Panel ruled breaches of Clauses 3.1, 9.1 and 2 of the Code.
The Panel ruled no breach of Clauses 4.1 and 4.9.

Breaches ruled in relation to failing to certify promotional material, failing to make clear the company’s involvement, and providing an inducement. No breach found for some clauses including Clause 2.
Breach of Clause 5.1; No breach of Clause 6.1
Breach of Clauses 2, 9.1, and 29. Public reprimand.

The Panel ruled that Janssen had promoted apalutamide for an off-licence use (metastatic CRPC) in breach of Clause 11.2, made misleading and unsubstantiated safety comparisons (Clauses 6.1, 6.2, 6.3, 6.4, 6.6, 14.1), failed to maintain high standards (Clause 5.1), and brought discredit upon the industry (Clause 2).
Breaches of Clauses 5.1, 5.5, 26.1, 26.2 and 2
The Panel ruled a breach of Clause 17.2 and no breaches of Clauses 17.4 and 17.5.
The Panel ruled breaches of Clauses 2, 5.1, 19.1 and 24.2 of the Code.

Panel ruled breach of Clauses 6.1 and 6.2 for the deposition claim, breach of Clause 12.1 for not providing Symbicort prescribing information, and no breach of Clauses 2, 5.1, 6.1, 6.2 or 12.1 for the spacer claim, and no breach of Clause 11.2.
The Panel ruled a breach of Clauses 6.1 and 5.1, no breach of Clauses 11.2 and 2.
No breach of Clause 5.1. Breach of Clause 26.2.
Breaches of Clauses 6.1 and 6.4 for claiming solutions are safe without appropriate qualification.
Breaches of Clauses 9.10 and 19.1 of the 2016 Code were ruled. No breach of Clause 2 was ruled.

The Panel ruled no breaches of the Code, including Clauses 2, 5.1, 3.6, 6.1, 10.1, and 11.2. The meeting was a legitimate LEMS meeting, the venue was not lavish, the booth material was not misleading, and the promotional material and tutorials were appropriate for the audience.
The Panel ruled that Otsuka Europe and Otsuka UK breached Clauses 2, 9.1 and 29 of the 2019 Code.

The Panel upheld complaints about Xeomin advertising claims regarding complexing proteins (Clause 7.2 breach) and claims about reduced risk of cold chain therapy failure (Clause 8.1 breach). The Panel also upheld complaints regarding claims suggesting comparable efficacy and 1:1 dosing interchangeability with Botox without adequate reference to non-interchangeability (Clauses 3.2 and 7.2 breaches). The Panel found the claims misleading, not sufficiently substantiated, and inconsistent with the product SPC.

The Panel ruled against Astellas on Clause 19.1, finding that the lavish venue (a luxury hotel in Hampshire with gourmet facilities and spa) and the requirement that all invitees attend all sessions constituted inappropriate hospitality that was not proportionate to the medical purpose. The Panel considered breaches of Clauses 2 and 9.1 as well, finding that the nature and scale of the hospitality compromised objectivity and was not appropriate for healthcare professionals attending an educational event.

The Panel found multiple breaches of the ABPI Code of Practice, including breaches of Clauses 9.1, 14.1, 15.9, 16.2, 7.10, 19.1, 16.1, 15.2, 3.2, 1.7, 1.8 and 2. The Panel upheld complaints regarding inadequate training on Code policies, failure to copy approve training materials, inadequate training on the Effentora Prescription Guide, lack of training on hospitality and other financial matters, and failure to maintain proper procedures for target lists to ensure compliance with licensed indications.

The Panel ruled against Astellas' complaint. While the Panel found some visual similarities between the Locoid and Eczmol advertisements, particularly in the use of animal imagery to convey a 'gentle/strong' message, it did not find that the Eczmol advertisement was an imitation likely to mislead or confuse in breach of Clause 9.4. The Panel considered that the differences between the advertisements (including the different animal compositions, tagline phrasing, color schemes, and the distinct positioning of elements) were sufficient to distinguish them. The Panel was not convinced that healthcare professionals would be misled into believing the products were interchangeable, particularly given that one was a corticosteroid and the other an antiseptic emollient with different therapeutic uses.

The Panel ruled that the claim 'only once-daily' was misleading in breach of Clause 7.2, as it could be read to suggest Lyxumia was the only once-daily GLP-1 receptor agonist available, when Victoza was also a once-daily option. The Panel also upheld complaints regarding cost-saving claims, finding them misleading under Clauses 7.2 and 7.3 as they failed to take account of comparative efficacy and safety data, particularly against Victoza. The Panel required amendments to ensure claims were fair, accurate and not misleading.

The Panel ruled that Leo Pharma had breached Clauses 7.2 and 9.1 of the Code. The Panel found that the promotional materials had been used in a manner that could circumvent local formulary restrictions, and that Leo Pharma had failed to ensure that its promotional activities were compliant with the Code's requirements regarding the responsible promotion of medicines and compliance with local arrangements.

The Panel ruled that the advertisement did not comply with the Code, finding a breach of Clause 5.1 because the non-proprietary name was not immediately adjacent to the most prominent display of the brand name and/or was not of the required minimum size.

Breach of Clause 7.2 – the letter incorrectly described CoCyprindiol as a combination of isotretinoin 20mg and erythromycin 250mg, rather than cyproterone acetate and ethinylestradiol; this was misleading information about a medicine.
The Panel ruled breaches of Clause 2, Clause 10, Clause 18.1 and Clause 18.4 of the 2006 Code.
The Panel ruled a breach of Clause 7.2 (Misleading information) and Clause 9.1 (Discrediting the industry). No breach of Clause 2 or Clause 7.4 was ruled.

The Panel ruled a breach of Clause 2 and Clause 9.1. Napp was found to have made misleading comparisons and failed to include relevant safety information about Targinact being a Schedule 2 controlled drug. The comparison of Targinact 10mg/5mg twice daily with 8 co-codamol 30/500 tablets and with tramadol 200mg daily was misleading and not supported by evidence. The Panel considered that the materials posed a risk to patient safety and brought discredit upon the pharmaceutical industry.

The Panel ruled a breach of Clause 15.2 (actions bringing discredit upon the pharmaceutical industry) and Clause 7.2 (misleading information). The representative's statement to the practice that the medicines management team was to be disbanded was incorrect and misleading. The company's response was limited because the complainant did not provide further information, but the Panel found the conduct constituted a breach.

Bayer advised that the advertisement was for doctors only and directed to use in other conditions was not intended. The Panel noted that the advertisement was for Yasmin, a combined oral contraceptive. The advertisement listed beneficial effects vs baseline on acne, fluid retention, hirsutism and premenstrual symptoms. The Panel noted that these conditions were not licensed indications for Yasmin. The Panel considered that the advertisement was misleading and not capable of substantiation. The Panel ruled a breach of Clause 7.2. The Panel noted that the advertisement asked doctors to prescribe Yasmin for conditions that were not licensed indications. The Panel considered that this was misleading and not capable of substantiation. The Panel ruled a breach of Clause 3.2. The Panel considered that the advertisement was inconsistent with the SPC, which listed acne, fluid retention and hirsutism as adverse events. The Panel ruled a breach of Clause 3.2. The Panel considered that the advertisement was not consistent with the SPC and was misleading. The Panel ruled a breach of Clause 2.

The Panel ruled a breach of Clause 3.2 as the MLS's email promoted Procoralan for an unlicensed indication (heart failure). A breach of Clause 9.1 was ruled as the conduct fell below the high standards expected. No breach of Clause 2 was ruled. The Panel also ruled a breach of Clause 15.2 as the MLS failed to maintain high standards.
Breach of Clause 7.2 and Clause 9.1. No breach of Clauses 3.2 and 4.1.
The Panel found breaches of Clauses 2, 3.1, 3.2, 9.1, 14.2, 14.3, 19.1 and 22.1.

The Panel ruled no breach of Clauses 2, 9 and 21. The Panel noted that the Code requirements related to disclosure of clinical trial results within a timeframe and that the complainant's study methodology and interpretation had been considered. The Panel did not consider that a breach of the Code had been established in relation to the disclosure of clinical trial results for Incivo (telaprevir).

The Panel ruled a breach of Clause 9.1. MSD had given a clear undertaking during inter-company dialogue to withdraw all materials associating alogliptin with the black triangle by the end of August 2018, and the continued use of such a material at a conference in October 2018 constituted a failure to honour that undertaking and a failure to maintain high standards.

The Panel ruled breaches of Clause 4.3 for omission of generic names in the webinar and meeting invitations, Clause 4.9 and 4.10 for omission of adverse event reporting statements and black triangles, Clause 26.3 for omission of adverse event reporting on the Ellipta patient leaflets, and Clause 7.2 for the exacerbation reduction claim presented as relative risk reduction without absolute risk reduction. The Panel found no breach of Clause 3.2 for the asthma meeting invitation as it concluded the invitation did not imply Trelegy was licensed for asthma. The Panel ruled breaches of Clause 9.1 and Clause 2 in relation to the cumulative failings. The cost-effectiveness claim was found to be inaccurate and misleading, with breaches of Clause 7.2 and 9.1 upheld. Clause 14.1 was breached in relation to materials not being properly certified.

Panel found GlaxoSmithKline in breach of Clauses 2, 3.1, 9.1, 26.1 and 29 for promoting an unlicensed product to the general public on LinkedIn and for breach of undertaking; the company was required to give a further undertaking.

The Panel ruled breaches of Clauses 2, 9.1, and 22.4. The LinkedIn post and website did not make clear Novo Nordisk's involvement or whether the meeting was promotional or non-promotional. The Panel considered that the PGD had a value and offering it to health professionals to run private clinics constituted an inducement to prescribe, which was unacceptable. The Panel was concerned about the overall arrangement and ruled a breach of Clause 2.

The Panel ruled a breach of Clause 5.1. The Panel noted that in Case AUTH/3281/11/19 the Appeal Board had ruled that the use of a premium rate telephone number for patients and members of the public to contact a company was unacceptable. The Panel considered that the use of an 0845 number for the Customer Care Centre for reporting adverse events was inconsistent with the requirements of the Code and ruled a breach of Clause 5.1. No breach of Clause 6.1 was ruled.

The Panel ruled breaches of Clauses 9.1, 29, and 2. Both Otsuka Europe and Otsuka UK were found in breach of Clause 9.1 (failure to maintain high standards) for the omission of 'monthly' from the prescribing information and the failure to identify this during approval. The Panel ruled a breach of Clause 29 (breach of undertaking) given the similarity to previous Cases AUTH/3041/6/18 and AUTH/3042/6/18 where prescribing information inconsistent with the SPC was used. The Panel also ruled a breach of Clause 2 (bringing discredit upon the industry) due to the repeated nature of the issue.
Breaches of Clauses 3.1, 4.1, 9.1, 26.1 and 28.1; no breaches of Clauses 2, 4.6 and 14.3
